name: Philip Cooney

summary.text: Philip Cooney, a lawyer and former lobbyist for the American Petroleum Institute, served as chief of staff of the White House Council on Environmental Quality under President George W. Bush. In June 2005 The New York Times reported, from internal documents, that he had edited government climate reports in 2002 and 2003 to play down links between greenhouse gases and warming; he resigned two days later and ExxonMobil confirmed it had hired him. The House Oversight Committee examined his edits in 2007 hearings and a December 2007 report.

facts.claim: Internal White House documents reported in June 2005 showed Cooney, chief of staff at the Council on Environmental Quality, had altered national climate reports in 2002 and 2003 in ways that played down the link between greenhouse gases and warming.
facts.quote: The paper said it had obtained internal White House documents showing he had altered national climate change reports during 2002 and 2003.

facts.claim: Cooney resigned two days after the documents surfaced; the White House defended his work.
facts.quote: He resigned two days after those documents surfaced.

facts.claim: Before joining the administration Cooney was a lawyer and lobbyist for the American Petroleum Institute and had no scientific training.
facts.quote: Before joining the administration, Cooney was a lawyer and lobbyist for the American Petroleum Institute, an industry group. He had no scientific training.

facts.claim: ExxonMobil confirmed in June 2005 that it had hired Cooney, to start in the autumn, without giving details of the job.
facts.quote: ExxonMobil confirmed it had hired him, but an Exxon Mobil spokesman declined to give details of the job, which was to start in the autumn.

facts.claim: At a January 30, 2007 House Oversight hearing Rick Piltz testified about Cooney's role in editing the Climate Change Science Program strategic plan and the report 'Our Changing Planet'; Chairman Waxman said in March 2007 that Cooney and his staff made hundreds of edits to the strategic plan, and Cooney testified he did not have final responsibility for several key documents.
facts.quote: Chairman Waxman's March 2007 statement said Cooney and his staff made hundreds of separate edits to the government's climate change strategic plan.

openQuestions: Site claim (documented; edited reports to play up uncertainty, resigned, joined ExxonMobil): supported. The site cites Wikipedia; the 2007 House Oversight hearing record on govinfo is the best primary source.
The often-cited figure of 181 edits was not confirmed from the sources used; Waxman's statement said 'hundreds'.
